If you’re new to resting heart rate, here is a quick guide.

Health is confusing, and overwhelming.

> a low resting heart rate before bed is good
> a high resting heart rate before bed is bad

+ asleep in less than five min

+ finish caffeine around noon

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Imagine a Scottish army surgeon in the 1790s telling a dying diabetic officer to skip the bread and eat blood pudding, old fatty meat, and rancid pork instead—and watching the sugar disappear from his urine.
That doctor was John Rollo. He trained in Edinburgh, joined the Royal Artillery as a surgeon in 1776, served in the West Indies, and later became Surgeon-General at Woolwich. 

Diabetes was rare and deadly then. Doctors knew the urine of some patients tasted sweet, thanks to earlier work by Matthew Dobson, but most treatments failed. 
In 1796 Rollo treated Captain Meredith of the Royal Artillery, a once-heavy man now wasting away. Rollo reasoned that the sugar in the urine came mainly from vegetable foods and decided to cut them back hard. 

He put Meredith on an “animal diet”: blood puddings made of blood and suet, game or long-kept meats, fatty and even rancid pork when the stomach could handle it, plus some milk mixed with lime water and a little bread and butter. He also used medicines to calm the stomach. 

Within weeks Meredith’s urine lost its sugar and he began regaining strength and flesh. When symptoms returned, Rollo tightened the diet further—dropping more of the milk and plant foods and switching to beef tea (meat broth). The patient improved again and returned to duty. Rollo published the case in 1797 and added more in 1798. He was among the first to systematically recommend a low-carbohydrate, meat-heavy diet for diabetes and is credited with helping popularize the term “diabetes mellitus.” 

His approach—restricting starches and sugars while emphasizing animal foods—became a standard treatment for more than a century until insulin arrived in the 1920s. Patients who stuck to it often lived longer and felt better. Rollo even noted that some did better when they avoided all vegetables for a time, and later allowed a few low-sugar greens like spinach or cabbage once the disease was controlled.
He died in 1809, but his meat-first idea showed that what people ate could change the course of diabetes long before modern drugs existed.
hits.draft_en:

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
A Giant Korean Study of 15 Million People Just Blew a Hole in the “Lower LDL Is Always Better” Story
Imagine tracking almost 15 million adults for nearly nine years and counting every death from heart disease and stroke. That’s exactly what Korean researchers did with 14.9 million people who weren’t even taking cholesterol drugs. What they found doesn’t match the simple message that “the lower your LDL, the safer you are.” Instead, the risk formed a U-shape. People with very low LDL died more often from cardiovascular causes, people with very high LDL also died more often, and the sweet spot sat right in the middle.
For overall cardiovascular death the lowest risk landed between about 90 and 149 mg/dL. Below that range or well above it, deaths went up. The pattern changed depending on the exact problem. For heart attacks and blocked arteries the best zone was lower (around 70–114 mg/dL). For some types of brain bleeds the risk kept falling only when LDL stayed higher. In plain terms, driving LDL as low as possible protected against one kind of death while raising the risk of others.
When the scientists looked only at the higher range (100 to 300 mg/dL) they still saw a clear rise in heart-attack deaths as LDL climbed. Each jump of about 40 mg/dL raised the chance of dying from ischemic heart disease by roughly 26 percent. But that rise was weaker in women and in older adults than in younger men. Even people in their late 70s and early 80s still showed some extra risk from higher LDL for heart attacks and ischemic strokes, yet the overall picture never became “lower is always safer.”
The study is huge, it followed real people instead of just guessing from lab tests, and it only looked at folks who were not already on statins. That makes the U-shape harder to wave away. Doctors still treat high LDL when people already have heart disease or several risk factors, because the top end of the curve is real. But the data also show that pushing every healthy adult toward rock-bottom LDL numbers is not free. Too low carried its own price in this massive population.
The takeaway is simple and uncomfortable: LDL cholesterol is not a one-way street. In nearly 15 million Koreans the safest zone for dying of cardiovascular disease was not the lowest number on the lab report. Both extremes cost lives. That single finding from one of the largest studies ever done keeps forcing the same awkward question—how low is actually low enough, and for whom?
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker is sharing a big Korean study: nearly 15 million adults not on cholesterol drugs, followed for about nine years.

What he says it found: the risk of dying from heart disease and stroke made a U-shape. Very low LDL and very high LDL both had more deaths, and the lowest overall risk sat in the middle, about 90 to 149 mg/dL. For heart attacks the best zone was lower, about 70 to 114. Higher LDL still raised heart-attack deaths, but less so in women and older people.

His point: "lower is always better" isn't the full story.

If you're over 50, don't stop or change any meds off a tweet. Take the question to your GP: how low is low enough for me?

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In the late 1950s, a German drug company told the world it had created the perfect sedative—one so safe that overdoses rarely killed and pregnant women could take it freely for morning sickness. Within years, more than 10,000 babies were born with missing or truncated limbs, their hands or feet sometimes emerging directly from their torsos. The drug was thalidomide. The scale of the disaster was driven by manufacturer negligence and regulatory systems that failed to demand basic safety evidence before approval.

Chemie Grünenthal developed and aggressively marketed thalidomide (Contergan) across Europe, Canada, Australia, and elsewhere starting in the late 1950s. Testing was inadequate even by the standards of the day: animal studies were limited or poorly designed, and no proper evaluation of effects on a developing fetus occurred, despite the drug’s promotion for pregnancy. The company claimed safety in pregnancy with scant supporting data. When reports of irreversible nerve damage in adult users emerged around 1959, Grünenthal minimized or denied the connection, delayed critical publications, and in some accounts used private investigators against complaining doctors and patients. Internal awareness of serious risks grew; critics, including later court documents and investigative reporting, allege the company continued sales for weeks after strong indications of birth-defect links (including an internal communication suggesting knowledge by mid-October 1961) and threatened researchers such as German pediatrician Widukind Lenz who first publicly connected the drug to the epidemic of malformations. Company staff and their families themselves had affected children. A 1968–1970 German criminal trial of executives ended without convictions—the court assessed individual culpability as minor—but still found that Grünenthal had not met the standards of a conscientious manufacturer regarding nerve damage. The company later funded compensation and issued a 2012 apology widely criticized by survivors as too little, too late.
Regulatory systems outside the United States were equally deficient. Approvals proceeded under frameworks that did not require teratogenicity testing or rigorous clinical data. In the United States, FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey repeatedly rejected the application on grounds of incomplete safety evidence, preventing formal marketing and limiting the toll (though investigational distribution still reached many patients). The contrast exposed systemic gaps elsewhere. Post-disaster reforms (including the 1962 U.S. Kefauver-Harris Amendments) mandated stronger efficacy and safety requirements, but they arrived only after thousands of children had been permanently harmed by a drug whose risks the manufacturer understated and regulators failed to catch.

He says the testing was poor, the warnings were played down, and regulators didn't demand the safety evidence. One US reviewer, Frances Kelsey, kept knocking it back and limited the damage there.

Worth remembering when someone tells you a new pill is completely safe. Ask what the evidence is.

The Rice Diet’s Dark Side: Forced Compliance
Walter Kempner’s rice diet was mostly white rice, fruit, and sugar. Patients got almost no salt, almost no fat, and only a tiny bit of protein. It tasted like nothing. Meals were the same every day. People felt hungry, bored, and weak. Most quit the second they left the hospital or the “rice houses” where staff watched them. The food was so dull that normal people could not stay on it for long. They missed real meals, salt, and the freedom to eat what they wanted.
Kempner did not rely on choice. He used fear. He yelled at patients who slipped. He checked their urine every day and sometimes posted the results for everyone to see. He took car keys and credit cards so people could not sneak out for forbidden food. When that was not enough, he used a riding crop. He admitted he whipped patients who broke the rules. He said some of them asked for it or agreed in advance. Duke University knew about the crop by the 1970s and told him to stop, yet he kept treating patients. A former patient later sued, claiming he whipped her bare skin and then controlled her life for years. He denied the worst parts. The case settled after he died. None of it was proven in court, but the whipping was not denied.
The diet only worked when people were locked into a system of constant watching, shame, and physical punishment. Take those tools away and almost no one stayed on it. The results came from extreme control, not from rice and sugar being a magic cure. Patients left the moment the pressure lifted because the food itself was miserable and the rules were brutal.

The FDA greenlit eating cotton seeds after scientists genetically silenced the plant’s natural poison.
In 2019 the agency finished its review of TAM66274 cotton from Texas A&M. This is a genetically engineered variety that uses RNA interference (a gene-silencing tool) so only the seeds produce almost no gossypol. Gossypol is the toxic compound cotton makes to fight insects. Regular cottonseed has roughly 10,000 parts per million of free gossypol. The new version drops that to about 260–300 ppm—under the FDA’s 450 ppm limit for human food. 
That decision means roasted cottonseed kernels, flour, and oil from these seeds can be sold as food. Promoters say the world produces enough cottonseed protein each year to cover basic needs for hundreds of millions of people, and the seeds taste a bit like chickpeas. Cotton plants already make more seed than fiber by weight, so the idea is to turn a byproduct into a dual-purpose crop without extra land. 
Cotton has never been grown primarily as a food crop. It is one of the most heavily sprayed crops on Earth because the fiber is the main product. Even refined cottonseed oil requires processing to strip out most of the gossypol and pesticide residues. The “safe” leftover gossypol is still there. At higher doses the same compound has been studied for decades because it can damage the heart, liver, and male fertility. Cottonseed proteins also share similarities with certain legumes and nuts, so allergy risk exists even if cottonseed is not on the official major-allergen list. 
The FDA’s conclusion was essentially “we have no further questions” after reviewing the university’s data. That is the same low bar used for many genetically engineered crops. Years later the trait still has not become a major commercial food ingredient in the United States; commercial interest has been limited and the technology is now being shared with partners such as Uzbekistan for possible humanitarian use. 
For anyone who prefers real food over novel plant proteins, this is another example of regulators opening the door to more ultra-processed ingredients from a pesticide-intensive, non-food crop. The marketing will talk about fighting malnutrition. The fine print is genetic engineering, residual toxins, heavy chemical use, and another industrial protein source competing with meat, eggs, and dairy.

Meat doesn’t destroy the microbiome. It rewires it—and the long-term data show the rewiring leaves diversity intact.
The “meat kills your gut bacteria” claim rests on short-term feeding trials that captured rapid shifts toward bile-tolerant species after a few days of all-animal food. Those snapshots were treated as proof of permanent damage. Newer work on people who have lived on carnivore diets for years tells a different story.
In a 2024 case study of a healthy man on a strict carnivore diet for four years, researchers found a microbiome dominated by Faecalibacterium, Blautia, Lachnospiraceae, Bacteroides, and Roseburia—genera classically labeled as fiber degraders. Alpha- and beta-diversity matched omnivore controls. Predicted functional capacity was comparable. The carnivore’s profile was actually least similar to people who ate meat daily on an otherwise standard diet. 
A 2026 cross-sectional study expanded this to ten healthy long-term carnivores (average adherence ~36 months) compared against 874 matched omnivore controls. Alpha-diversity was not reduced; the carnivores showed higher Chao1 richness, meaning more low-abundance taxa. There were no significant losses of Akkermansia muciniphila, the Lactobacillus group, or butyrate-related pathways. Taxonomic shifts occurred—enrichment of Synergistetes and Desulfobacterota, reductions in some Bifidobacterium and specific Faecalibacterium and Roseburia species—but the diet itself, not age, BMI, or lifestyle, drove the differences. Functional modules moved toward amino-acid degradation, vitamin B synthesis, energy metabolism, and protein fermentation. The authors noted the results challenge the assumption that dietary fiber is required to maintain microbiota diversity. 
Clinical observations line up. A 2024 case series of ten patients with confirmed ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease reported large gains on the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Questionnaire after switching to mostly carnivore or carnivore-ketogenic diets. Several had failed multiple other diets and stayed in remission for years off medication. Low-residue eating has long been used in IBD; these cases simply extend that pattern to a zero-plant extreme. 
The microbiome is adaptive, not fragile. Meat-heavy diets change which microbes thrive and which metabolic pathways dominate, but the available long-term human data show preserved richness and retention of key taxa and functions. The destruction narrative was an extrapolation from short-term shifts. The longer view does not support it.

Hong Kong: the place that eats the most meat, lives the longest, and ranks among the smartest.
While much of the West is told that meat shortens lives and dulls minds, Hong Kong does the opposite. FAO data puts its per-capita meat supply among the highest in the world (around 123 kg in recent years, with pork alone often exceeding 50 kg). For years it ranked at or near the absolute top. Cantonese cuisine is built on pork, chicken, and seafood, not on the “plant-forward” plate now pushed by dietary guidelines. 
At the same time, Hong Kong posts some of the highest life expectancies on the planet. Provisional 2025 figures show women at 88.7 years and men at 83.3. Overall expectancy sits near 86 years—consistently in the global top tier, often ahead of Japan and other celebrated longevity nations. 
Cognitive measures tell the same story. Large-scale IQ testing data places Hong Kong at the top of the rankings (recent International IQ Test figures around 107.7), with East Asia as a whole dominating the upper end of the distribution. 
This is not a one-off curiosity. A 2022 ecological analysis of 175 countries and territories found a strong positive correlation between total meat intake and life expectancy at birth (r ≈ 0.71). The relationship held after controlling for total calories, GDP, urbanization, obesity rates, education, and carbohydrate-crop intake. Carbohydrate crops showed weak or negative associations. The authors concluded that nutrition science that ignores meat intake will systematically mis-predict human lifespan. 
None of this proves that meat is the sole cause. Wealth, medical systems, low smoking rates, and urban density all matter. But the pattern is hard to dismiss: the population that eats the most meat also lives the longest and scores among the highest on cognitive metrics. That is the opposite of what mainstream dietary guidelines and plant-based advocacy have predicted for decades.
If the data keep pointing in the same direction, the burden of proof shifts. Hong Kong is living evidence that high meat consumption is compatible with—and may actively support—exceptional longevity and cognitive performance.

John Kopchinski didn’t just quit a sales job. He torched the corporate script.
A West Point graduate and Gulf War veteran who served as a military police platoon leader on the Saudi-Kuwait border, Kopchinski was personally hired by Pfizer’s then-CEO after corresponding from the desert. By 2003 he was a top sales rep in Florida pushing Bextra, a painkiller the FDA had approved only for narrow uses and limited doses. Management wanted more: off-label promotion for surgical pain, migraines, and higher doses that later contributed to its withdrawal over cardiovascular risks. A $50 bounty for getting doctors to add it to pre- and post-op protocols. High-dose samples handed to specialists who weren’t treating menstrual pain. The message was clear—hit the numbers or you’re not a team player.
Kopchinski refused. With a baby son and twins on the way, he filed a qui tam suit under the False Claims Act after being fired for raising the issue. Six years of depleted 401(k)s, a drop from $125k to $40k, and blackball risk later, his case helped produce Pfizer’s then-record $2.3 billion settlement (including a $1.3 billion criminal fine for Bextra marketing) and a felony plea. His personal share: more than $51.5 million. He stayed in the same San Antonio house and still split one large popcorn at the movies.
The industry treated the settlement as a rounding error. Sales culture didn’t fundamentally change; it just got more careful about documentation. Off-label promotion, speaker programs, and the quiet pressure on reps didn’t vanish—they evolved. Kopchinski’s line still cuts: “In the Army I was expected to protect people at all costs. At Pfizer I was expected to increase profits at all costs, even when sales meant endangering lives. I couldn’t do that.”
Most reps never get the chance—or the stomach—to say the same thing out loud. The ones who do usually pay for it long before any check arrives. The system still counts on that math.

Monkeys Are Getting Fat, Sick, and Diabetic From Too Much Fruit Sugar — And Scientists Can Prove It
Picture this: scientists put a bunch of healthy monkeys on a diet loaded with fructose — the same sugar that makes fruit sweet — and watched what happened. Within months the monkeys started packing on fat. Their livers filled up with greasy deposits. Their bodies stopped handling sugar properly. Some even crossed the line into full-blown diabetes. These weren’t wild monkeys swinging through the jungle. These were controlled experiments that show exactly what happens when primates (and that includes us) get too much sugar and too little real work.
In one study, cynomolgus monkeys ate a high-fructose diet for years. Their livers got fattier the longer they stayed on the sugar. Fat built up inside the liver cells, and over time the liver started to scar. The fructose-fed monkeys were also much heavier than the ones who didn’t get the extra sugar. Another experiment gave rhesus monkeys a fruit-flavored fructose drink every day for a year. Every single monkey developed signs of metabolic syndrome: extra body fat, insulin resistance, and messed-up blood fats. About 15% of them became diabetic.
Captive monkeys get into the same trouble without fancy lab diets. Zoos and research centers often feed them commercial chow plus supermarket fruit that is way sweeter and lower in fiber than anything they’d find in the wild. The result is the same pattern: chubby monkeys with fatty livers and rising blood sugar. One famous example is “Uncle Fatty,” a macaque in Thailand who ballooned to twice the normal size because tourists kept handing him sweet melons, corn, and other sugary treats all day. He wasn’t sick from some rare disease. He was just eating more sugar than his body could handle while sitting around.
Wild monkeys almost never get this fat or develop fatty liver disease. The fruits they eat in the jungle are smaller, less sweet, and higher in fiber, and the animals are constantly moving. When you take the same animals, lock them up, and flood them with concentrated fruit sugar and easy calories, the damage shows up fast. Their bodies turn the extra fructose into liver fat, their insulin stops working right, and weight piles on. The experiments make the point clear: too much fruit sugar is not harmless. It drives the same metabolic problems in monkeys that doctors see in humans who drink sodas, eat candy, or load up on sweet fruit juice and dried fruit every day.
The takeaway is simple and uncomfortable. Monkeys prove that high intakes of fructose and easy carbs can make primates fat, damage their livers, and push some of them into diabetes. If it happens to them under controlled conditions, it’s hard to pretend the same process doesn’t happen to people who live on sugary food and sit still.

Today’s Fruit Is Basically Candy That Grew on a Tree
Your grandparents’ apples and bananas were not as sweet as the ones in the store right now. Farmers spent decades breeding fruit to be bigger, softer, and packed with more sugar. The result is fruit that looks healthy but delivers a sugar load much closer to soda than the wild versions animals used to eat. Zoos even stopped giving most fruit to monkeys and other animals because the modern versions made them fat and rotted their teeth.
Bananas are a clear example. Old British food records from the 1950s and 1960s show a typical banana had about 16 grams of sugar per 100 grams. Today’s numbers are higher, with some reports putting the increase around 25 percent from breeding aimed at sweetness. Apples and pears followed the same path. Older data showed their sugar levels roughly doubling over earlier decades, and U.S. figures once listed apples at 8–10 percent sugar before some climbed toward 15 percent. Watermelons, grapes, cherries, and peaches have also moved up the sweetness scale as breeders chased higher Brix scores.
The main driver is deliberate selection. Growers keep the sweetest plants and discard the sour or bland ones. Lower acidity and bitterness make the fruit taste even sweeter. Warming temperatures and modern storage methods help lock in more sugar too. When Melbourne Zoo’s head vet looked at the problem, he said cultivated fruits had been changed to contain far more sugar than their ancestral versions. Primates and red pandas were gaining weight and losing teeth, so the zoo switched them to leafy greens and nutrient pellets.
Wild fruit is still smaller, more fibrous, and less sugary. The supermarket version is the product of human choices aimed at making people buy more. That does not make whole fruit the same as a candy bar, but it does mean the sugar content is no longer the same as it was a century ago. The numbers show a clear shift toward sweeter fruit, and the animals in zoos noticed it first.

What if the surge in autoimmune disease isn’t mainly bad luck or rogue genetics—but a controllable failure of the gut’s security system?
Alessio Fasano, the Italian-born pediatric gastroenterologist, Harvard professor, and director of the Mucosal Immunology and Biology Research Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, has spent decades building the evidence for exactly that idea. While researching cholera in the 1990s, his team identified a bacterial toxin (zonula occludens toxin, or ZOT) that loosens the tight junctions between intestinal cells and increases permeability. Searching for the human counterpart, they discovered zonulin in 2000—the primary known physiological modulator of those same tight junctions. 
In genetically susceptible individuals, certain environmental triggers (most famously gluten in celiac disease) drive excess zonulin release. The barrier opens, antigens and other molecules cross into the body, and the immune system can tip from tolerance into chronic inflammation and autoimmunity. Fasano’s framework—the triad of genetic predisposition, an environmental trigger, and increased intestinal permeability—explains why not everyone who carries risk genes develops disease. His group showed elevated zonulin and increased permeability often appear before clinical disease in models of celiac disease and type 1 diabetes, and that blocking the pathway can interrupt the process. 
A 2003 epidemiologic study he led established that celiac disease affects roughly 1 in 133 Americans—orders of magnitude higher than earlier estimates—and helped redefine gluten-related disorders more broadly. The same permeability mechanism has since been linked to multiple sclerosis, other autoimmune conditions, and elements of neurodevelopmental and metabolic disease. Current work from his lab continues to examine the interplay of zonulin, the microbiome, and immune regulation across these conditions. 
The implication is practical as well as conceptual: if barrier dysfunction is an early, rate-limiting step rather than a late consequence, restoring or protecting that barrier becomes a plausible target for prevention and treatment. Fasano’s research turned “leaky gut” from fringe speculation into a measurable, mechanism-based contributor to chronic inflammatory disease.

Imagine turning on the evening news and hearing a friendly voice say, “Ask your doctor about this little pill,” before the anchor even mentions the weather. That never used to happen. For most of television’s history, drug companies were not allowed to sell prescription medicines straight to regular people on TV the way they do today.
For decades, the rules were strict. Companies could talk to doctors, but if they wanted to advertise a prescription drug to the public on television, they had to list nearly every risk and side effect in the commercial itself. That took too long for a 30-second spot, so almost no one tried. The rare early attempts, like a 1983 ad for a prescription pain medicine, got pulled almost immediately.
Everything changed in 1997. The Food and Drug Administration loosened the rules for TV and radio. Companies still had to mention the biggest risks, but they could point people to a website, an 800 number, or their doctor for the rest of the details. Suddenly, the floodgates opened. Spending on these “ask your doctor” ads shot up from a few hundred million dollars a year to several billion. Only the United States and New Zealand allow this kind of advertising for prescription drugs.
These ads do more than sell pills. They preload viewers. They plant the idea that everyday problems—trouble sleeping, feeling a little sad, high cholesterol, or stiff joints—need a brand-name medicine. Studies show that when patients walk into the doctor’s office already asking for a specific advertised drug, they are more likely to walk out with a prescription for it, even when a cheaper or safer option might work just as well.
The ads also shape the news itself. Drug companies spend huge amounts of money advertising on news programs, which reach older viewers who take more medicines. News outlets that depend on that advertising money have less incentive to dig hard into stories about drug side effects, high prices, or company misconduct. The result is a cycle: the same companies that sell the drugs also help pay for the shows that talk about health. Viewers end up hearing more about new pills and less about questions that might slow those sales down.

Vegans Break Bones a Lot More Often — And a Huge Study Proves It
A big group of scientists followed tens of thousands of people in Britain for years and counted every broken bone. The people who ate only plants broke far more bones than the people who ate meat. The difference was especially huge for hip fractures. Vegans were more than twice as likely to snap a hip as meat-eaters. That is not a small gap. That is the kind of gap that puts older people in wheelchairs and nursing homes.
The study is called EPIC-Oxford. It tracked meat-eaters, fish-eaters, vegetarians, and vegans. After the researchers adjusted for age, smoking, exercise, and even body weight, the vegan group still came out on top for fractures. Their total fracture risk was about 43 percent higher. Their risk of breaking a leg was roughly double. Hip fractures were the worst. Vegans had more than twice the chance of breaking a hip compared with people who ate meat. That works out to about 15 extra hip fractures for every 1,000 vegans over ten years.
Why does this happen? Vegans in the study ate less calcium and less protein on average than meat-eaters. Both nutrients help build and keep strong bones. Many vegans also weighed less, and thinner bones break more easily. Some of the risk stayed even after the scientists tried to account for calcium and protein intake. The numbers did not disappear. Long-term vegan diets, especially without careful supplements, leave bones weaker.
Doctors already know that broken hips are dangerous for older adults. Many people never walk the same way again. Some die within a year. The EPIC-Oxford numbers show that choosing a strict vegan diet raises that risk in a measurable way. The people who ate meat, fish, or even dairy and eggs had lower fracture rates. The gap was clear and it survived the usual excuses.
The message is simple. A diet that cuts out all animal foods can cost you bone strength. The largest long-term data we have shows vegans break more bones, especially the ones that matter most in old age. That is not theory. That is what the numbers say.

A New York Doctor Once Told Sick Patients to Eat Steak Three Times a Day — And Many Got Better
In the early 1900s a physician named Blake Donaldson watched his overweight patients fail on the usual low-calorie diets. They stayed hungry, weak, and stuck with the same problems. So he tried something different. He told them to eat fatty meat, mostly steak, three times a day, drink water and black coffee, and move their bodies. Over decades he claimed this simple plan helped people lose weight and ease diseases that doctors still struggle with today.
Donaldson worked as an internist in New York and later wrote a book called Strong Medicine. He believed humans had thrived for most of history on fresh fat meat and clean water. When people got into trouble with their health, he said, the smart move was to go back to that basic food. His patients ate about a half-pound of fatty meat at each meal — often steak or lamb chops with the fat left on. He banned sugar, flour, and a list he called the “big bad seven,” which included milk, cream, eggs, cheese, and chocolate. Exercise and a daily walk were part of the plan too.
He reported that many patients lost two or three pounds a week without feeling starved. More important to him, the weight stayed off better than with strict calorie cutting. He also said symptoms of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart trouble, gallstones, and allergies improved for a large number of the people he treated. Over roughly forty years he claimed to have used the approach with thousands of patients. A surgeon even wrote a supportive preface for his book. Critics called the idea unscientific food faddism, but Donaldson kept using it because he saw results in his office.
His core idea was simple and blunt. Obesity and the diseases that travel with it often improve when people stop eating the modern junk and stick to fatty meat. Whether every claim holds up under today’s standards is still debated. What is clear is that a practicing doctor more than a century ago built his treatment around the idea that steak and water could reverse serious health problems better than the low-fat, low-calorie advice of his time.

hits.text:
The FDA Helped Purdue Pharma Turn a Powerful Pain Pill Into a National Disaster
In the mid-1990s the FDA signed off on a new opioid called OxyContin and let Purdue Pharma tell doctors it was safer and less addictive than other pain drugs. That claim was wrong. Within a few years the pills were flooding small towns, people were getting hooked, and overdose deaths started climbing. The agency that is supposed to protect the public had green-lit the very product that helped start the crisis.
Purdue sold OxyContin as a long-acting pill that released the drug slowly, so patients would not get the quick high that leads to addiction. The FDA accepted that story and allowed the company to put language on the label saying the controlled-release design made abuse less likely. Doctors read those words and wrote millions of prescriptions. Later investigations showed the slow-release claim did not stop people from crushing the pills or taking extra doses. The FDA had not demanded strong studies proving the drug was actually safer before it hit the market.
While the pills spread, warning signs piled up. Pharmacies reported suspicious orders. Patients showed up in emergency rooms. Some FDA staff later moved into high-paying jobs at drug companies, including ones tied to the opioid business. Critics said the agency treated Purdue more like a partner than a company that needed tight oversight. When abuse became impossible to ignore, the FDA did tighten rules and add warnings, but by then the damage was already huge. Hundreds of thousands of Americans died from opioid overdoses in the years that followed.
Purdue itself pleaded guilty to criminal charges for lying about the risks and paid billions in settlements. The company is gone, but the FDA still faces hard questions about how it approved the drug, why it believed the company’s claims so easily, and why it took so long to act once the body count started rising. The record shows an agency that trusted the manufacturer too much, required too little proof, and left ordinary people to pay the price.
The lesson is blunt. When the government agency in charge of drug safety lets a company market a powerful opioid as less dangerous than it really is, the result is not just a bad product. It is a public-health catastrophe that lasts for decades.
